title: How to Make a TikTok Ad for Your Store | AIVideosUGC
description: Make your first TikTok ad from one product photo: pick one reason to buy, open on the product in action, post a vertical 9:16 video, launch on a small budget.
h1: How to Make a TikTok Ad When You've Never Made One
lead: Booking a creator for your first TikTok ad can cost more than the product earns. This guide takes one phone photo of your product to a vertical, ready-to-post ad you can launch this week, with no filming, actor or edit suite.
summary: Plan one clear reason to buy, turn a product photo into a vertical 9:16 video, add captions and licensed sound, and launch a first TikTok ad on a budget you control.

sections.h2: Pick one product and one reason to buy
paras: First ads often try to say too much, which costs attention and money. Choose one product and finish this sentence: "People buy this because..." Keep the answer short and specific.

"A phone stand that folds flat enough to slip into a jacket pocket" is a strong reason. "High quality, versatile, and stylish" isn't, because there's nothing to show. That specific answer gives you a clear scene to plan.

A few more examples: a candle that burns evenly to the bottom of the jar, a dog leash with a clip you can open with one hand, a lunch box with a lid that doesn't leak when tipped. Each one points to a scene you can picture.
sections.alt: Adult woman applies cream from a plain light-peach tube to her cheek at the seaside.

sections.h2: Plan the first two seconds around the product
paras: People scroll [TikTok](page:plat-tiktok) fast. If the opening doesn't give them something to watch, they're gone before your product appears, and you've paid for a skipped impression. Skip logo intros and slow fades.

Openings that hold attention show the product doing something right away: a hand snapping the phone stand open, [a drink poured over ice](page:tpl-drink), a sneaker turning to show its sole. Pick one moment that matches your reason to buy.
sections.alt: Two adult hands spread white cream from a plain peach tube across the back of a hand.

sections.h2: Turn your product photo into the video
paras: This is the step that replaces the shoot. In the Video Ads tool, upload a clear photo of the product and write one sentence describing the scene, such as "A hand unfolds a slim black phone stand on a cafe table and sets a phone in it, soft daylight." Choose 9:16, the full-screen vertical shape TikTok uses. The [ad sizes guide](page:guide-ad-sizes-by-platform) explains the other shapes. A [lifestyle product photo](page:lifestyle-photos) can give the same campaign a still image for the feed.

Then pick a length: 6, 10, 15 or 30 seconds. Six seconds suits a single moment, like the stand snapping open. Ten seconds leaves room for a short demo. Fifteen seconds fits a simple sequence, unfold, place the phone, start a video call. Thirty seconds fits a longer sequence. A video costs 24, 40, 60 or 120 credits depending on length, and the cost appears before the video starts; failed jobs refund the credits automatically.

Each run makes one video, so trying a second opening costs one more job, not another booking or shoot day. Run it again with a changed sentence, keep the request about the scene, and leave prices and headlines out. You'll add those next, where you control every letter.
sections.alt: Adult hands hold a plain peach sunscreen tube over a blank notebook on a bright cafe table.

sections.h2: Add text, captions and sound in TikTok or CapCut
paras: Open the video in TikTok's editor or CapCut. Add one short line near the start that names the benefit, like "Folds flat. Fits your pocket." Then add the price or offer if you have one.
Keep all text in the middle of the screen. TikTok places the account name, the caption, and the like and share buttons along the bottom and right edge, and they cover anything underneath.
Add sound in the same editor. For ads, pick from TikTok's Commercial Music Library or another source licensed for business use, since many songs people use in regular posts aren't cleared for ads.
sections.alt: One adult hand smooths white cream along a forearm beside a plain peach tube.

paras: Most TikTok ads are watched with the sound off first, so confirm the product and main text still make sense on mute; then listen with the sound on to make sure the track is clear.

Then ask a few plain questions. Is the product on screen within the first second? Can you read every word without pausing? Do the color and version in the video match what the product page sells? Is the price in the ad the same as the price at checkout?
If any answer is no, fix it now. A mismatch between the ad and the product page is one of the fastest ways to waste a click you paid for.
sections.alt: Adult hands turn one plain peach sunscreen tube for a pre-launch check.

sections.h2: Launch small and let the numbers choose
paras: In TikTok Ads Manager, create a campaign with a goal that matches what you want, such as traffic to your store or sales. Set a daily budget you're comfortable spending while you learn, send viewers to the product page for the item in the video, and add a clear button like "Shop now."
Write the ad caption the way you'd text a friend about the product: one line, plain words, no wall of hashtags. For the phone stand, "Fits in your pocket, holds your phone at eye level" says enough.

Let it run for a few days before you judge it. Look at how many people watch past the first few seconds, how many click, and what each sale costs. If you made a second opening, compare both in the same group of ads and see which one people stay with. The [guide to testing ad versions](page:guide-testing-ad-versions) shows how to compare them fairly, so every round gets cheaper insight instead of another expensive shoot.
sections.alt: Adult hands hold a plain peach sunscreen tube beside a notebook on a bright desk.

checklist: One product and one specific reason to buy
An opening that shows the product in action
Text and price added in TikTok or CapCut, away from the edges
A small budget and a few days before you decide

faq.q: How can I compare two TikTok openings?
faq.a: Make two versions with the same product, offer, and destination. Change only the opening, then compare the results in Ads Manager. Each version is a separate video job, so you see its credit cost before committing.

faq.q: Do I need to label an AI-made video on TikTok?
faq.a: Yes. TikTok asks advertisers to label realistic AI-generated content, and Ads Manager includes a setting for it when you create the ad. Policies change, so read [TikTok's current ad policies](https://ads.tiktok.com/help/article/about-ad-disclaimers-in-tiktok-ads-manager?lang=en) before you launch.

faq.q: What should I add after downloading the TikTok ad?
faq.a: Add captions, licensed sound, price, and call to action in TikTok or CapCut. Upload the finished 9:16 file in TikTok Ads Manager.

faq.q: How is this cheaper than booking a UGC creator?
faq.a: One photo and a written sentence replace the creator fee, the studio or location, and the edit round. A video costs 24 to 120 credits depending on length, and you can make a different opening in minutes without rescheduling anyone.

faq.q: Can I use the finished video as a paid ad commercially?
faq.a: Yes. Videos you make are yours to use in ads and on your store, and the delivered file has no watermark. Keep the source photo of the real product yours, and follow TikTok's current advertising policies.

faq.q: What file shape should my first TikTok ad use?
faq.a: Use a 9:16 vertical file for a full-screen TikTok ad. Keep captions, offer text and buttons clear of the interface edges.

cta_title: Post your first TikTok ad this week
cta_lead: Turn one product photo into a 9:16 ad, add your offer in the editor, and launch it in TikTok Ads Manager.
